story.title: Trump Expresses Support for a Unified Ireland During Visit
story.summary: During his visit to Ireland, President Donald Trump stated that he would 'love' to see Ireland reunified, calling it 'fantastic' and 'inevitable.' His comments were made while attending the Irish Open golf tournament and meeting with Irish leaders, including Micheál Martin. Trump suggested that reunification could happen soon, despite Downing Street's commitment to the Good Friday Agreement.

explore_lenses.label: Did Trump’s remarks change the process?
explore_lenses.title: No legal mechanism changed
explore_lenses.summary: Trump’s intervention was a political statement, not a change to the constitutional process. Northern Ireland’s status remains governed by the Good Friday Agreement and UK law.

claims.text: Under the Northern Ireland Act 1998, the Northern Ireland secretary may call a unity referendum and must do so if it appears likely that a majority of voters would back leaving the UK for a united Ireland.
A referendum cannot be ordered less than seven years after a previous referendum held under that schedule.
The Good Friday Agreement makes consent central to Northern Ireland’s constitutional status and commits both governments to respect identities and rights regardless of the outcome.

points: Under the Northern Ireland Act 1998, the Northern Ireland secretary may call a unity referendum and must do so if it appears likely that a majority of voters would back leaving the UK for a united Ireland.
A referendum cannot be ordered less than seven years after a previous referendum held under that schedule.
The Good Friday Agreement makes consent central to Northern Ireland’s constitutional status and commits both governments to respect identities and rights regardless of the outcome.
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The statute does not define a precise evidentiary threshold for deciding when a pro-unity majority is 'likely'.

explore_lenses.label: How do London, Dublin and nationalists differ?
explore_lenses.title: Agreement on consent, disagreement on timing
explore_lenses.summary: The principal stakeholders broadly invoke the Good Friday Agreement, but differ over who should judge whether conditions for a vote have been reached and how quickly the question should move forward.

claims.text: Trump said he would like to see a unified Ireland and forecast that it would happen eventually; he also acknowledged that the UK would have a role in the matter.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was not aware of majority support for another referendum and that one would not occur unless that changed.

Taoiseach Micheál Martin said it was unsatisfactory for the referendum trigger to rest solely on the Northern Ireland secretary’s judgment; he called for Dublin, London and Northern Ireland parties to discuss the threshold and cautioned against a hasty vote.

Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald previously argued that no British prime minister could remove the unity-referendum provision from the Good Friday Agreement after Burnham had described the issue as off the table.

story_report.summary: President Donald Trump voiced support for Irish reunification during a visit that included meetings with Irish leaders and attendance at the Irish Open golf tournament. He said he would like to see a unified Ireland, calling the prospect “fantastic” and “inevitable,” while also acknowledging that the United Kingdom would have a role. The comments placed a U.S. presidential forecast alongside an active dispute over when Northern Ireland could hold a vote on its constitutional future.

sections.heading: Northern Ireland Referendum Rules
sections.body: The Northern Ireland Act 1998 allows the Northern Ireland secretary to call a referendum on leaving the UK for a united Ireland, and requires one if it appears likely that a majority would support that outcome. A further referendum cannot be ordered within seven years of a previous vote held under that process. The Good Friday Agreement places consent at the center of Northern Ireland’s constitutional status and commits the British and Irish governments to respect identities and rights regardless of any outcome.

sections.heading: Leaders Differ on Referendum Timing
sections.body: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was unaware of majority support for another referendum and said one would not take place unless that changed. Taoiseach Micheál Martin said it was unsatisfactory for the trigger to depend solely on the Northern Ireland secretary’s judgment, urging discussions among Dublin, London and Northern Ireland parties while warning against a rushed vote. Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald has said the Good Friday Agreement’s referendum provision cannot be removed by a British prime minister.

related_stories.summary: Leaders of the BRICS nations, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping, convened in New Delhi for a summit focused on trade, investment, and global conflicts. The meeting aims to enhance the bloc's influence in shaping the global agenda for emerging and developing countries.

related_stories.title: Tributes to 9/11 Victims at Republican Convention in Dallas
related_stories.summary: At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, tributes were paid to the victims of the September 11, 2001 attacks.
